The Stellar Archive
By ADAPTED WORK

Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive Project was a cursed venture leased for a mysterious tour of the outer colonies. It made a one-night installation on a Marvenia research station—to find that sabotage stalked it from the shadows in corrupted data streams.

Matthew Fisher leaned forward across the small conference table. He knocked over the mug of synthetic coffee, but it didn't matter. The mug was empty. He jabbed me in the shoulder with his stylus, not very hard. Not hard enough to actually hurt, just enough to make his point.

"We," he said, "are finished. Bankrupt. Out of funding and out of options." He added, as an afterthought, "Destitute."

I looked at him. I said sourly, "You're exaggerating!"

"Exaggerating." Matthew put his elbows on the table and peered at me through a curtain of very dark hair that needed cutting. "She says I'm exaggerating! With Fisher's Digital Humanities Archive, the Greatest Cultural Repository in the Colonies, so deep in debt..."

"It's no deeper in debt than you are in denial." I was irritated because he'd been hogging the coffee dispenser all morning. "The Greatest Cultural Repository. Please! I've managed Fisher's Digital Archive around the Woodbridge Region for seven years, and I know. It's underfunded, it's understaffed, it's breaking down! Nothing works, from the quantum computing servers to the junior archivists. In short, it's failing!"

I must have been more tired than I thought. Nobody insults Matthew Fisher's Digital Archive to Matthew Fisher's face unless they're exhausted and want a long argument.

Matthew stood up. He stood up slowly. I had plenty of time to see his brown eyes narrow, and hear the soft hum of the environmental controls, and watch the curious stares of the station personnel at nearby tables swing toward us, interested and somewhat amused.

I had plenty of time to think how I'm not as diplomatic as I should be, and how Matthew has a temper when pushed.

I said, "Matthew. Wait. I..."

Somebody said, "Excuse me. Is one of you Dr. Matthew Fisher?"

Matthew put his hands on the table. He closed his eyes and smiled tightly and said, very carefully:

"Would you be here about the server lease, or the data storage fees?"

I shot a glance at the newcomer. She'd saved me from an uncomfortable confrontation, even if she was a creditor; and I felt sorry for her. Matthew Fisher straightened his shoulders like he was preparing for battle.

The stranger was petite. She made even me look tall. She was dressed in dark-grey professional attire, very conservative. There was a touch of grey in her dark hair and her skin was pale, smooth, and carefully maintained. She had the kind of face that university administrators will trust with sensitive projects. I looked for her security detail.

There didn't seem to be any. The woman looked at Matthew with pale grey eyes, and her voice was softer than his.

She said, "I don't think you understand."

I felt uneasy, suddenly. Somebody shifted in their seat. The sound was loud in the quiet cafeteria. I straightened up, and my palms were damp. Matthew Fisher sighed.

Then I saw what the woman was holding in her hand.

I stood up quickly. "Wait," I said. "Look at that."

Matthew glared at me. "What's wrong with you, Samantha? I'm handling this."

"Shut up," I said. "Look what she's got there. A funding authorization!"

The woman looked at me. She hadn't reacted at all. "Yes," she said. "A funding authorization. Quite substantial. Would you permit me to join you?"

Matthew Fisher sat down. He managed a more genuine smile. "Of course. I'm Dr. Fisher. This is Samantha Boyd, my project manager." He looked at the spilled coffee. "I apologize for that. Misunderstanding."

The woman smiled slightly. She did it with her lips. The rest of her face remained professional and unreadable, almost mask-like. I realized with a start that it wasn't a mask at all. It was the most complete poker face I'd ever encountered, and you couldn't read those calm grey eyes any more than you could read encrypted data.

I didn't trust her. I didn't trust her at all. But she had funding. I said, "Hello. Let's find a private meeting room. These station personnel make me nervous, watching like they're waiting for entertainment."

The woman nodded. "Excellent suggestion. My name is Margaret Kim. I wish to—ah—commission your archive services."

I looked at Matthew. He looked more hopeful than he had in months. We didn't say anything until we got Margaret Kim into a private conference room with fresh coffee on the table. Then I cleared my throat.

"What exactly did you have in mind, Ms. Kim?"

Kim sipped her coffee, made a polite face, and set it down. "I have access to independent funding sources. It has always been my mission to preserve cultural heritage for future generations..."

Matthew got tense. "Just a moment," he murmured, and started to stand. I touched his arm.

"Let Ms. Kim finish."

He sat down, looking suspicious. Kim ignored him. She continued, quietly,

"I have always believed that oral history preservation, properly executed, is the most valuable service we can provide to humanity's collective memory..."

I said, "Of course. But what was your specific proposal?"

"There are many settlements along the Marvenia frontier where no systematic cultural documentation has been conducted. I propose to remedy that. I propose to commission your archive, Dr. Fisher, to make a tour of several colonies in the outer territories."

Matthew had relaxed. His eyes began to show interest. He started to speak, and I interrupted.

"That would be expensive, Ms. Kim," I said. "We'd have to postpone several other projects..."

She looked at me. I was stretching the truth, and she knew it. But she said,

"I quite understand. I would be prepared..."

The door slid open suddenly. Kim stopped talking. Matthew and I turned to look at the figure in the doorway.

It was Miguel Ortiz, our senior technician—a tall, intense man from a Terran colony on Mars. I'd visited once. Miguel looks a lot like the landscape there—serious, uncompromising, and tough. His hands, gripping the doorframe, were stained with equipment grease and were nearly as large as maintenance tools.

He said, "Boss, the quantum computing array is acting up again."

"The array can wait," said Matthew. "Can't you see I'm in a meeting?"

Miguel's dark eyes were worried. "I'm telling you, Boss, the system isn't stable. It hasn't had proper maintenance. If something..."

I said, "That'll all be taken care of, Miguel. Please give us a moment."

He looked at me like he was calculating how much trouble I was causing. "Fine! But the system's unstable. It's overheating, understand? And if it doesn't get proper attention soon I'm not sure our backup protocols will hold."

He left, letting the door slide shut with emphasis. Matthew Fisher groaned. Kim cleared her throat and said, rather formally,

"The quantum computing array?"

"Yes. It's somewhat temperamental." Matthew took a quick sip of coffee. I elaborated.

"It's the backbone of our archive operations, Ms. Kim. A state-of-the-art quantum computing system. The only other comparable system in the region belongs to the University Consortium, and theirs is much smaller than ours."

Theirs was also much newer, but I didn't mention that. Our array may be outdated, but it's still impressive. I only hoped it wouldn't fail completely, because without it we'd have a more dysfunctional operation than even I could tolerate.

Kim looked impressed. "A quantum computing array. How fascinating! The applications for digital humanities research must be extraordinary. The processing capabilities..."

We were getting off track. I said tactfully, "We'd need at least fifty thousand credits."

It was twice what we had any right to ask. I was prepared to negotiate. Kim looked at me with that unreadable expression. For a fraction of a second I thought I saw something behind her calm grey eyes, and my instincts screamed warning. Kim smiled professionally.

"I'm not inclined to haggle. Fifty thousand Universal Credits will be acceptable." She produced a tablet, entered some commands, and displayed an authorization code.

"By way of initial funding. My legal representative and I will meet with you tomorrow morning with a formal contract and project timeline. Good evening."

We said good evening, trying to contain our relief. Kim departed. Matthew reached for the tablet to verify the authorization, but I was faster.

"Wait," I said. "There are creditors waiting for this. Serious creditors with legal claims. Here." I transferred a small amount to a discretionary account. "We can celebrate with this."

Matthew has an extensive vocabulary. He used it. When he caught his breath he said suddenly,

"Kim is running some kind of operation."

"Obviously."

"It may be illegitimate."

"Possibly. And she may be eccentric and genuine. For heaven's sake!" I said. "You want to sit here until the project collapses completely?"

Matthew looked at me, oddly. He looked at the tablet in my hands. He ran his fingers through his dark hair.

"Yeah," he said. "I hope there'll be enough left to pay the lawyers." He moved toward the door. "Hey, let's get Miguel. We need to discuss this!"

It was quite late when we returned to the aging research station where Fisher's Digital Archive was housed in its cramped quarters. Late as it was, they were waiting for us. About fifteen of them, sitting around the common area and looking very unhappy.

It was lonely out there, with the station's recycled air cool and stale, carrying that faint metallic taste of old environmental systems. There's a feeling to these outer stations, like something abandoned and waiting. An uneasy feeling. The fluorescent lights flickered occasionally.

Matthew Fisher walked into the common area where our team had gathered. He was steady enough. He waved and said, "Hello, everyone."

They stood up from their workstations and chairs and came toward us. I straightened and prepared for confrontation. We felt we owed these people more than just apologies. It grates on a person's pride to have to avoid their own team members in the corridors. This was the first time in weeks we'd faced them directly.

I displayed the funding authorization on my tablet. That stopped them. Very formally, Matthew and I explained the situation, outlined the payment schedule, and answered questions. Matthew stretched and looked genuinely relieved.

"Well?" he said.

"Well," I said.

We had a productive discussion. Some people were skeptical. We addressed their concerns. Everyone felt better afterward. They had assurance of payment, and we had their renewed commitment.

The news spread through the station quickly. The junior archivists and the data specialists and the oral history researchers and all the other dedicated but underpaid professionals that make up a digital humanities project were noticeably more optimistic, discussing the possibilities over dinner.

Matthew Fisher regarded them with satisfaction, wiping fatigue from his eyes. "They're good people, Sam. Excellent colleagues. They stayed with me, and I'm going to make it right."

I said, "Sure," rather wearily. Matthew looked thoughtful.

"Let's check on the quantum array."

I didn't want to check on the quantum array. I never felt comfortable in the server room, especially at night or during system maintenance. I'm a people person, myself. The hum and heat of high-powered computing gives me anxiety. But Matthew looked determined, so I shrugged.

"Okay. But just for a minute. Then we need sleep."

"You're a good colleague, Sam. Best project manager anywhere..."

The argument had worn him down. I was worried he'd make a mistake and damage something expensive. That's why I went along. If I hadn't... Oh, well, what's a few sleepless nights among colleagues?

It was dim in the server room. At the far end, there was a soft blue glow. Miguel was evidently monitoring the quantum array. We started down the long corridor between the rows of server racks and cooling units and backup systems.

Our footsteps echoed on the metal floor. I wasn't as confident as Matthew, and my skin prickled with unease. It's the sound, I think; the constant hum and the occasional clicks and whirs. And the sense of them, these powerful machines processing endless streams of data, with their patient indifference contained by cooling systems and surge protectors.

Matthew Fisher stumbled slightly. I caught his arm, and then wiped sweat from my forehead despite the cool air. An alarm sounded. A sharp, piercing warning tone that cut through the mechanical ambiance. The quantum array, experiencing critical errors.

It had been stable. Now every monitoring system activated simultaneously. My stomach dropped. I called out every technical term I could think of, and I couldn't hear myself over the alarms. Presently a loud electronic tone silenced the warnings. Miguel had triggered the emergency shutdown.

But the systems didn't stabilize. Not really. They were compromised. You can sense it when systems are compromised. I think that's why I'm anxious around them. They make me feel vulnerable—like our entire project could disappear in an instant. Yeah. They were compromised that night, suddenly...

Miguel looked grim as we reached the main console. "It's getting worse," he said. "Someone's been accessing the system."

"That's concerning," said Matthew Fisher. His eyes looked tired. He swayed slightly with exhaustion. "That's very concerning." He frowned.

I looked at the quantum array. Its housing was the largest and most sophisticated in the facility and even so it looked like it could fail catastrophically at any moment. I don't know if you've ever seen a quantum computing array in crisis. There are only a few in the outer colonies. If you haven't, nothing I can say will convey the anxiety.

They're what the tech specialists call "bleeding edge technology." Seems the engineers had ambitious ideas about quantum computing. The arrays were quite successful initially, but something always causes problems and now there's only a few operational, way out in the research facilities, where even the maintenance crews rarely go. Expensive experiments.

I couldn't help feeling worried about it. The array was housed in its protective chamber with its cooling systems—yes, multiple redundant systems—working overtime and its processing cores deep in their quantum states, executing calculations. Just calculating. Not for anything specific. The status displays showed unstable qubits, like warning fires.

The ambient light was blue-white on the metallic housing, but the error indicators made the monitoring displays flash red, showing system failures. It looked like a disaster waiting to happen.

Miguel said quietly, "Someone's been tampering with it. And somebody needs to fix this properly."

Matthew frowned. I said irritably, "Be reasonable, Miguel! Nobody outside the team has access. There must be a logical explanation."

The alarm sounded again. The array didn't move, obviously, but the temperature readings spiked. The warning, that close, was deafening, and it made me feel cold and hollow inside. The danger, the sheer technical catastrophe...

Matthew Fisher looked shaken. I said, "You'll have to stabilize this, Miguel. It's threatening the entire archive."

He worked on the emergency protocols, and things stabilized somewhat. Miguel stood looking at the monitoring displays, checking readings carefully, like a diagnostician. Then he turned to us.

"I've been maintaining this system," he said. "When we salvaged it from the university surplus and everyone thought it was too damaged to use, I rebuilt it. I know this array. I can work with it. But this time..."

He shrugged. He was large and intense and serious, and his voice carried genuine concern.

"This time," he said, "I'm not certain we can recover."

"Well for Pete's sake, do what you can. We have a contract, and we need it operational." I took Matthew's arm. "Come on, we need rest."

He leaned on my shoulder and we left. Miguel didn't acknowledge us. Matthew looked troubled.

"You were right, Sam," he mumbled. "Project's in trouble. I know it. But it's my life's work. I care about it, Sam. Understand? Like Miguel there with the array. It's old and problematic, but he maintains it. I care..."

"I know," I told him. "Stop worrying for one night."

We were far from the server room then. The racks and systems loomed high and dark around us. It was quiet. The subtle, uneasy hum all around us and our footsteps only made it quieter.

Matthew was nearly asleep on his feet. I started to guide him back. And then I noticed something on a nearby terminal—small traces of unauthorized access, barely visible in the system logs.

I called out, "Miguel! Miguel, there's been a security breach! Miguel—we need you!"

I started to return to the server room. Matthew leaned heavily on me, exhausted. The alarms burst suddenly in a deafening cascade of warnings and error messages, amplified by the metal walls, and above it all I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems screaming in overload.

I thought, "Someone's here. Someone caused this. Someone wants to destroy us!" I tried to call out again. It caught in my throat. I was sweating, and it was cold.

Matthew's stumbling steps tangled with mine. We fell. I caught him, protecting his head, and braced myself against a server rack.

The first system failure hit. It was like an electrical shock, a cascade of shutdowns spreading through the network. I shouted. The failures propagated through the connected systems.

Matthew groaned and struggled. I remember holding on and thinking, "This is it. This is the end, and I'm terrified!"

Then everything went dark.

---

Emily Gutierrez, our station medic, was checking my vital signs when I woke up. Her round face showed concern. She'd worked double shifts recently, and she looked exhausted.

"You're okay, Ms. Boyd," she said gently. "You'll be fine."

She gave me something for the headache. It helped. I asked, "Where's Matthew? How is he?"

"Dr. Fisher is fine. You protected him from injury. You're quite the hero, Ms. Boyd. Miguel got the systems shut down in time. You're a hero."

I said, "Right," and pushed myself up carefully. I managed to stand, though I felt dizzy. I made it to the small mirror in my quarters—I was in my own room—and I saw I looked exhausted but uninjured.

Matthew Fisher opened the door. He looked pale and serious, and there was a bruise on his arm. He said:

"Kim is here with her legal representative."

I found my jacket. "I'll be right there."

Emily left, still looking concerned. Matthew closed the door.

"Sam," he said, "those systems were stable when we arrived. Someone deliberately compromised them. On purpose."

I felt terrible. I said, "Obviously. Nobody saw anything, I suppose?" Matthew shook his head.

"Question is, Sam, who wants to sabotage us, and why?"

"Kim. She realizes she's made a mistake funding us."

"Fifty thousand credits," said Matthew quietly, "for some remote colony documentation work. It doesn't add up, Sam. You think we should withdraw?"

I shrugged. "You're the director. I'm only the one who manages the creditors."

"Yeah," Matthew said thoughtfully. "And I hear unemployment isn't pleasant. Okay, Sam. Let's go sign." He reached for the door and looked at me. "And—uh—Sam, I..."

I said, "Forget it. Next time, just don't trip over me, that's all!"

We had a difficult journey to Goldfield, Marvenia. The quantum array remained unstable, and Miguel, on the rare occasions he emerged from the server room, looked like he was expecting catastrophe. To make it worse, Jacob Anderson, our lead oral historian, fell ill during transit, and one of our junior archivists quit unexpectedly.

Nobody would have minded that, except she took copies of sensitive research data with her. It lasted just long enough to terrify that group of paranoid academics. Digital humanities people are peculiar that way.

Matthew and I did some quiet investigating, but it was futile. Anyone on the team might have sabotaged those systems. It didn't help to know that somebody, maybe the person working next to you, was planning to destroy everything. By the time we reached Goldfield, I was ready to resign entirely.

Matthew guided our transport to the edge of Goldfield, the first location on our itinerary. I stood beside him, looking at the settlement through the viewports. It was Marvenia, certainly. Red dust and scattered prefab structures and harsh sunlight, and a cluster of weather-beaten buildings grouped together defensively. People in environment suits were approaching for a look.

I saw Kim's sleek corporate shuttle parked at a dedicated landing pad, and our equipment transport beside it. Matthew groaned.

"A disaster, Sam. A complete disaster!"

I muttered, "What do you expect, with this underfunded project!" and exited. He followed. The team was gathering near the airlock, but they weren't enthusiastic. You develop instincts for these things. The thin Marvenia atmosphere was already infiltrating through the seals.

As we passed the corridor to the server room, I could hear the quantum array's cooling systems, struggling.

The technical crew was busy setting up equipment, working carefully in the harsh environment. The documentation team was heading for the settlement. Matthew and I stood in our environment suits, observing.

I heard a sound behind me and turned. Angela Perry, our xenoanthropology specialist, was standing in the dust with her helmet off, breathing the thin atmosphere, and her weathered face tilted back, eyes closed. She was smiling. It looked unsettling.

You find many xenoanthropology specialists in digital humanities projects, studying cultural adaptation in frontier settlements. They're colonial specialists, they're not typical academics, and they never let you forget it.

Angela opened her sharp eyes and looked at me and laughed.

"Failure," she whispered. "Failure and conflict. The settlement warns me. I can sense it in the atmosphere."

The harsh sunlight beat down on her. She shivered despite the heat, and her expression was intense.

"The frontier colonies are resistant," she whispered. "Something has been disturbed. They are resistant, and I sense failure ahead!"

She walked away, laughing, and I cursed under my breath, and my stomach was tight. Matthew said,

"Let's see if they have a cafeteria in this place."

We weren't halfway across the landing area when a man emerged from a building at the settlement's edge. We could see him clearly, because he was separated from the crowd approaching us.

He stumbled in the dust, calling out. It took him several attempts to make our names clear enough to understand.

Matthew said, "Sam—that's Jacob Anderson."

We started running. The crowd, mostly rugged colonists in work clothes, turned to see what was happening. People began to converge on the man who staggered and gasped in the thin air.

Jacob Anderson was an oral historian, collecting cultural narratives from frontier communities. He'd collaborated with us several times previously, when funding allowed, and we had a good working relationship.

I hadn't seen him for two years. I remembered him as energetic and enthusiastic, passionate about preserving oral histories. I felt sick, looking at him now.

Matthew tried to help him. Anderson was shaking, trembling like someone in shock. Some colonist stepped forward and offered him water from a canteen.

I was focused on Anderson then, and I didn't pay attention to the colonist. I only glimpsed the person's face briefly. I didn't realize until later that they looked familiar.

We got Anderson inside the building. It turned out to be a small community center, with a few private meeting rooms at the back. We got him into one and closed the door on numerous curious faces. Anderson drank from the canteen. The person who gave it to him had disappeared.

Matthew said gently, "Okay, Jacob. Relax. What happened?"

Anderson tried to compose himself. He hadn't slept. The energetic lines of his face had gone slack and his eyes were red-rimmed. He was covered with dust, and his hands shook.

He said hoarsely, "I found it. I said I would, and I did. I found it and documented it."

He set down the canteen clumsily. "Help me," he said simply. "I'm frightened." His voice broke.

"I have it secured. They want to locate it, but I won't tell them. It needs to be returned. Returned to its source. I tried to do it myself, but they prevented me, and I was afraid they'd find it..."

He reached suddenly and gripped the edge of the table. "I don't know how they discovered it, but they did. I have to return it. I have to..."

Matthew looked at me. Anderson was pale and sweating. I felt frightened, suddenly. I said, "Return what where?"

Matthew stood. "I'll get the medic," he said. "Stay with him." Anderson grabbed his wrist. Anderson's fingers were white and the veins in his hands stood out prominently.

"Don't leave me. Need to tell you—where it is. Need to return it. Promise you'll return it." He gasped, struggling for breath.

"Of course," said Matthew. "Of course we'll return it. What is it?"

Anderson's face was terrible. I felt nauseated, watching him fight for air. I wanted to get Emily anyway, but somehow I knew it was too late. Anderson whispered,

"Cultural artifact. Irreplaceable. Original. You don't understand...! Return it."

"Where is it, Jacob?"

I reached past Matthew suddenly and opened the door. Kim was standing there. Kim, leaning forward, clearly listening. Anderson made a harsh choking sound and collapsed across the table.

Kim's expression didn't change. She didn't move while Matthew checked Anderson's pulse. Matthew didn't need to speak. We knew.

"Heart attack?" said Kim finally.

"Yes," said Matthew. He looked as shaken as I felt. "Poor Jacob."

I looked at the canteen on the table. I looked at Kim with her unreadable professional face. I moved past Matthew and firmly guided Kim into a chair.

"Keep her here until I return," I said.

Matthew stared at me. Kim started to object. "Be quiet," I told her. "We have a contract." I left the room and walked to the main area.

I began to notice something then. There were quite a few people in the center. At first glance they looked appropriate—a weathered, capable group of colonists in practical clothing.

Then I looked more carefully. They were dressed appropriately enough. But they moved wrong for frontier colonists, on Marvenia or anywhere else.

The place was unnaturally quiet. The center administrator was a heavy-set woman with calculating eyes and short grey hair. She looked nervous.

I approached the counter. "Water," I said. She provided it, reluctantly, from a dispenser. I reached for it, casually.

"That man we brought in," I said. "He seems very distressed. Dehydrated. What's he been doing out here?"

"Research," said a voice beside me. "As if you didn't know."

I turned. The person who had given Anderson the canteen was standing next to me. And I recognized them, then.

The Chronicles of the Crystal Throne

In the mystical realm of Xandria, where magic flowed through the very stones and ancient trees whispered secrets to those who would listen, there existed a tradition as old as the realm itself: the Ascension Speeches. Every time a new monarch took the Crystal Throne, they would address their subjects from the Luminous Balcony, their words recorded by the Memory Scribes in enchanted tomes that preserved not just the text, but the very essence of the moment.

Sophie Leonard, a young scholar at the Academy of Temporal Studies in Oakdale, had spent the last three years of her life studying these speeches. The current ruler, Queen Lucia Page, was about to deliver her second Ascension Speech after renewing her bond with the Crystal Throne, and Sophie had been commissioned to write a comprehensive analysis of all previous speeches for the Royal Archives.

As Sophie sat in her tower study, surrounded by glowing manuscripts that floated gently in the air around her, she marveled at what she had discovered. There had been fifty-three Ascension Speeches since the first Queen, Rosa the Wise, had taken the throne in what the common folk called the Year of First Light. Each speech was worth studying—not just the famous ones like Rosa's founding address, the speeches of King Vincent the Unifier during the Great Schism, or Queen Juliana's rallying cry during the Shadow Wars. Reading them gave Sophie a peculiar sensation, as if she were standing in those ancient moments, not as a scholar of the present looking back through centuries, but as an ordinary citizen who shared the hopes, fears, and limited understanding of those distant times.

Among all the past monarchs and their counsel of advisors, there had been only one who possessed what the realm called the Gift of True Speech: King Vincent Hart, who ruled during the Shadow Wars. His second Ascension Speech, delivered after the realm had been nearly torn apart, still brought tears to the eyes of any who read it, even after two hundred years. The magical resonance embedded in the words themselves could make one's blood run cold with its power and beauty. None of the other speeches possessed such raw magical potency, though they were dignified and thoughtful addresses given by capable rulers, each attuned to their era's needs and conscious that their ascension was the most sacred moment of their reign.

Sophie had noticed that the tone and approach of the speeches seemed to fall into three distinct phases. The first, lasting until King Vincent's time, was characterized by what she termed "the humble servant style." The second phase, continuing through Queen Samir Zhang's reign, took on a more administrative character—what Sophie called "the managerial monarch approach." The third phase, which began with King Miguel Ortiz and continued to the present day, embodied what she described as "the visionary leader-prophet style." This classification wasn't perfect, of course. Some rulers seemed to bridge categories, and individual circumstances sometimes demanded departures from the prevailing style. But the overall trend was unmistakable.

When Sophie first examined Rosa the Wise's inaugural speech, she was immediately struck by its modesty. Rosa had been chosen unanimously by the Council of Elders, the first time in recorded history such agreement had been reached. She was more revered than any subsequent monarch at the moment of their ascension. And yet, what did she say?

"The weight and complexity of this sacred duty, to which the voice of our people has called me, being sufficient to cause even the wisest and most experienced among our citizens to question their worthiness, must surely overwhelm one who—possessing only modest gifts from the Source and untrained in the arts of realm governance—ought to be especially aware of her own limitations."

None of her successors expressed such profound humility, though echoes of it appeared in nearly every speech for the next three centuries. The one exception was King Luis Hughes, Rosa's immediate successor, who seemed so envious of Rosa's legacy that he spent much of his speech enumerating his own considerable qualifications and magical abilities.

That era of deep humility ended with King Vincent. Subsequent speeches routinely contained expressions of modesty, but they felt perfunctory, lacking the sincere vulnerability of the earlier monarchs.

Sophie theorized that this early modesty served multiple purposes. It reflected the courtly etiquette of the time, certainly, but it also addressed specific political concerns. In the realm's early centuries, many citizens feared that the monarchy might transform into a tyranny, with the ruler becoming more dictator than servant. Later, perhaps after the Reformation of the Second Age, a new anxiety emerged. The southern provinces, particularly around Cliffside in Fendria, had developed distinct cultural practices and systems of local governance. They worried that central authority might be used to interfere with their autonomy. The monarchs' assurances of limited power may have been intended to comfort these regions.

King Vincent faced an entirely different situation. With the Shadow Wars threatening to tear the realm apart, he could only fulfill his sacred duty to "preserve, protect, and honor the Ancient Covenant" by asserting the full authority of the Crystal Throne and his own power as sovereign. It was no time for self-deprecation. Vincent's successors inherited a monarchy with far greater centralized authority—and more need to exercise it—than had existed before the wars. They had less motivation to minimize themselves and their powers.

In the third phase, the Ascension Speech transformed from describing governmental policy to inspiring the people's behavior and consciousness. Monarchs recognized—or at least believed—that the realm faced challenges they ought to address but could not solve through governmental action alone. This represented a shift in consciousness studies and cultural sociology within the realm.

Thus, in his first speech, King Miguel Ortiz proclaimed: "At last, a vision has been granted to us of our realm in its entirety. We see the corruption alongside the virtue, the decay alongside the vitality. With this vision, we approach our future."

If the realm suffered from moral decay, the cure had to come from elevating the people's consciousness, not merely from royal decrees. Similar diagnoses and prescriptions appeared in later speeches.

Monarchs derived their authority to serve as visionary leader-prophets from an observation made by Queen Samir Zhang, though not in her Ascension Speech. She had remarked that the Crystal Throne was "a sacred platform for teaching," a metaphor that suggested not just written proclamations but direct magical and spiritual connection between ruler and subjects. The development of the Resonance Crystals—and even more so, the Vision Pools—made this possible across the entire realm. A telltale sign of the leader-prophet style was the repeated use of the phrase "Let us..."—meaning, effectively, "Follow my guidance." This expression appeared occasionally throughout the history of speeches, but it became dominant in recent centuries. King Luis Grant used it eighteen times in his Ascension Speech, and Queen Rosa Porter repeated it twenty-four times in her second speech.

The change in literary style from formal classical language to more accessible common speech could be demonstrated statistically. In all speeches from Rosa the Wise through King Thomas the Mediator, the average sentence contained sixty-two words. From King Vincent through Queen Samir, it dropped to forty-five words, and in the modern era it averaged thirty-four words. Sophie didn't consider this a decline in quality—her own scholarly writing averaged about twenty-three words per sentence—but it reflected changes in the audience and communication methods. Early monarchs could reference obscure magical theorems and ancient philosophical texts, expecting their audience to understand. That wouldn't be true today. But those ancient audiences wouldn't have understood references to theoretical modeling in consciousness studies or behavioral economics in trade policy.

Sophie discovered that monarchs and their advisors often borrowed memorable phrases from their predecessors without attribution. King Luis Grant's famous rallying cry, "Ask not what magic the throne can work for you; ask what magic you can work for the realm," had an ironic history. In his speech, King Thomas the Builder—hardly a model for the charismatic Luis—had said, "Our most dangerous tendency is to expect too little of our rulers while doing too little for our realm." And even before his ascension, Thomas had proclaimed in a speech at the Academy, "In our great destiny, we must have citizens less concerned with what the throne can do for them and more devoted to what they can do for the realm."

Many issues had their moment in Ascension Speeches before fading into history. These included the Dragon Accords, the Coastal Shield Barriers, territorial expansion into the Wildlands, the Great Canal project, reform of the Guild system, regulation of necromancy, and prohibition of blood magic. Some subjects that Sophie expected to find were conspicuously absent. King Samuel's speech, delivered just before the Great Economic Collapse, contained no hint of financial vulnerability. Queen Juliana's second speech, given as dark forces gathered in the Shadow Realms, made no reference to the coming war. But what amazed Sophie most, reading from her perspective in the modern era, was the near-total silence regarding the rights of the Fae-touched—those born with mixed human and Fae ancestry.

The word "Fae-touched" didn't appear in any speech until Queen Samir's first address, and even then only as part of the phrase "humans and Fae-touched," never acknowledging their specific concerns or the discrimination they faced. Even King Thomas, the first monarch chosen in an election where Fae-touched citizens could vote throughout the realm, didn't remark on this historic change in his speech.

One subject that received consistent attention was taxation and financial regulation. "Taxes" or equivalent terms appeared in forty-five of the fifty-two speeches. King Marcus said in his speech: "The time approaches when we can reduce the tax burden. I oppose extremely high rates, for they generate little revenue, harm our prosperity, and are fundamentally unjust." Royal taxes then consumed about four percent of the realm's economic output. King Rafael said essentially the same thing three centuries later, when taxes claimed twenty-two percent.

The most troubling aspect of the entire collection of speeches was what was said—and left unsaid—about the treatment of the Shadowborn, those born in the cursed regions of Shadowbrook Town and surrounding territories. The words "Shadowborn," "cursed ones," or "shadow-touched" didn't appear at all until King Jonathan's speech in the Year of Reconciliation. Queen Elizabeth the Prosperous had asked rhetorically in her speech, "Upon whom has injustice fallen in any corner of our realm? Who has been denied their rights or property?" These questions were meant to elicit the answer "No one!"—as if there weren't thousands of Shadowborn living in bondage, denied basic human rights, their very existence considered a stain upon the realm.

Before the Shadow Wars, the word "bondage" appeared only in the speeches of King David the Cautious and King Robert the Reluctant, and then only to argue that, pursuant to ancient law and to preserve realm unity, the system should not be challenged. But although generally unmentionable, the issue was reaching a crisis point, and would explode into the Shadow Wars.

After the wars, it was in the speeches of King Jonathan, Queen Catherine, and King William that Sophie found the most explicit discussion of the need to transform into reality the rights and freedoms granted to the Shadowborn on paper by the Three Great Edicts. Catherine's speech was particularly forceful on this point. She had studied at the Academy in Oakdale during an era when it had been a sanctuary for escaped Shadowborn, and her commitment to human rights ran deep. But then the subject began to fade from the speeches. King Alexander said in his first speech, "The persecution of Shadowborn must not be tolerated in a great and civilized realm such as ours," but he said it without passion or urgency. Queen Victoria raised the subject only to express satisfaction at the progress that had been made. And then it vanished. Queen Juliana never mentioned it in any of her four speeches, despite reigning during a period of renewed discrimination.

After the Restoration, the subject returned to Ascension Speeches, but in vague, abstract terms. This was true even of monarchs Sophie knew had been deeply concerned with Shadowborn rights—like King Marcus, Queen Helena, and the current Queen Lucia. Perhaps each felt they had made a sufficient statement by having a prominent Shadowborn perform at their ceremony—a famous singer, a celebrated mage, or a renowned poet. In Queen Lucia's first speech, the only allusion to Shadowborn rights was this sentence: "From our founding, through the Shadow Wars, the Great Collapse, and the Rights Movement, our people have always found the strength to build from these crises the foundations of our future." Sophie noted this not to suggest their concern wasn't genuine, but to indicate what was considered acceptable to say in a speech intended to appeal to values shared by all citizens.

There was much more to contemplate in these speeches than Sophie had summarized in her analysis. There was much to take pride in—the realm's endurance through countless challenges, the peaceful transfer of power through the Crystal Throne's magic, and the general wisdom of the monarchs the people had chosen. But there was also a lesson in humility to be learned. Sophie looked back with astonishment at the ignorance and moral blindness revealed in what past leaders had said and past citizens had believed. She recognized that fifty or one hundred years hence, scholars would shake their heads at what her own generation was saying and believing.

As Sophie prepared to attend Queen Lucia's second Ascension Speech, she wondered what future scholars would make of this moment. What would they see that she was blind to? What injustices of her own time would seem obvious to them but remained invisible to her?

She gathered her notes, extinguished the floating manuscripts with a wave of her hand, and made her way down from her tower. The ceremony would begin at sunset, and she had been granted the honor of standing among the Memory Scribes to record this historic moment. As she walked through the ancient streets of Oakdale toward the palace, she passed citizens of all kinds—humans and Fae-touched, merchants and mages, even a few Shadowborn who had made their way from the southern territories. They were all heading in the same direction, drawn by the same anticipation.

Whatever Queen Lucia would say from the Luminous Balcony, whatever vision she would cast for the realm's future, it would become part of the great tapestry of Ascension Speeches. And someday, perhaps centuries hence, another scholar would sit in a tower study, surrounded by glowing manuscripts, trying to understand what this moment had meant and what it revealed about the consciousness of the age.

Sophie smiled at the thought. The work of understanding never ended. Each generation had to grapple with the wisdom and folly of those who came before, while remaining humble about their own limitations. It was the scholar's burden and privilege—to preserve the past, illuminate the present, and leave questions for the future.

As she approached the palace gates, the first stars began to appear in the darkening sky, and somewhere in the distance, ceremonial bells began to ring, calling the realm to witness another chapter in its long, complex, and continuing story.
